scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The origins of ball de bastons are attributed by folklorists to prehistoric agricultural rites, Greek pyrrhic dances, or evolutions of ancient sword battles.

It is documented as the oldest traditional dance still performed in Catalonia, Aragon, and Valencia, with its earliest recorded mention dating to 1150 at the wedding banquet of Count Ramon Berenguer IV.
Widespread by the 15th century, it shares historical roots with European traditions like English and Welsh Morris dancing and Portuguese dança de pauliteiros.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The choreography symbolizes ritual combat between two opposing sides, alternating battle motions with intricate geometric intercrossings.
Originally an exclusively male ritual, women began participating in the 1960s and now play a major role, although specific towns like Montblanc maintain traditional male exclusivity.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers perform in double rows of 8 to 24 people, executing short choreographies of about one minute.
Key figures include 'pasadas' (crossing paths while striking), 'bajocamas' (clashing sticks underneath a raised leg), high aerial jumps to strike sticks, and striking the ground.
Role-specific mechanics divide dancers into 'derecheros' (who block strikes using their right arm) and 'izquierderos' (who strike using their left arm).
Watch for pasada, bajocama, batacada.

Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Opposed double lines, inner/outer rotating circles ('cadena'), or four-person quadrangles ('cuadras').

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Melodies are primarily built on easy 2/4 rhythms played on tabor pipe, shawm, or bagpipes.
Historical tunes from this tradition, such as 'Villano de Zamora', served as popular grounds for European Renaissance and Baroque music composers.
Listen for the tabor pipe, shawm, gralla, bagpipes.
The pulse is 2/4 at about 120 beats a minute.
Bright, piercing wind melodies driven by shawms or tabor pipes, punctuated by acoustic percussive clashing of solid oak sticks on every beat.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Traditional attire consists of white shirts, white trousers or velvet pants, colored waist sashes, a decorative short skirt (faldellín), colored chest handkerchiefs designating the group, and traditional 'espardenyes' (espadrilles).
The sticks are traditionally made of dense holm oak wood, measuring 40–50 cm (16–20 inches) long and 5 cm (2 inches) thick.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key individual roles within the performance group include the 'cabeza de cola' who directs the ensemble, and the 'banderero' (flag-bearer) stationed at the end of the line carrying a flag in the left hand and a single stick in the right hand.
Known as 'danzas de paloteo' in Castile and León and Aragon, and 'bastonets' in Algemesí where it takes the form of a warrior dance.

Traced back to medieval sword and weapon dances, documented continuously in Catalonia since 1150 CE, and preserved today through regional 'colles bastoneres' across Catalonia, Valencia, Aragon, and Castile and León.

scenes.title: Body and posture
narration: Upright, alert athletic stance with knees slightly flexed to absorb leaps and rapid directional changes.
Firm grip on one or two wooden sticks, executing defensive blocks with the right arm or offensive strikes with the left arm.
Square to partner, stable core with dynamic torso rotation during crossing moves.
